findings.title: Retry-count cleanup deletes workflow reminders outside the intended SMS failure scope
findings.body: The deleteMany query deletes any WorkflowReminder with retryCount greater than 1 because the second OR branch is not scoped to method: WorkflowMethods.SMS or scheduled: false. This can remove EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminders, or an SMS reminder already marked scheduled with a referenceId, if retryCount ever exceeds 1. That can cause unintended data loss and orphaned provider messages. The branch should be limited to unscheduled SMS reminders, e.g. { method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }.

findings.title: retryCount is incremented from a stale read instead of atomically
findings.body: Both failure paths set retryCount to reminder.retryCount + 1 using the value read before the scheduling attempt. If two cron executions overlap, or the row is updated between the read and write, increments can be lost or overwritten. This can cause more than two attempts, premature deletion, or incorrect cleanup state. Use Prisma's atomic update, e.g. data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }.

findings.title: Unsendable reminders with no message or recipient never increment retryCount
findings.body: If message is empty or sendTo is falsy, the reminder is skipped without incrementing retryCount, marking it scheduled/cancelled, or deleting it. A permanently unsendable reminder, such as one with a missing phone number, will be fetched and skipped on every cron run until scheduledDate passes, bypassing the intended delete-after-two-failures behavior. This case should increment retryCount or explicitly cancel/delete the reminder.

findings.title: Error handler can throw while trying to increment retryCount
findings.body: In the catch block, the retryCount update is not protected from failure. If the reminder was deleted concurrently or the update otherwise fails, the update error masks the original scheduling error and aborts processing of the remaining reminders. Using updateMany or wrapping the retry-count update in its own try/catch would make the cron job more resilient.
